title: The Shape Fear Makes
logline: A six-pointed star of granite and coral, drawn on paper after a fort was lost and built in two years so that nothing could come near any of its faces unseen — and for two hundred and sixty years nothing has.
human_question: If the thing I am braced against never arrives, what is left standing where the bracing was?

place.what_kind_of_place: Two colonial-period defence works in the far south of the island, fifty kilometres apart, and neither of them the big famous one. The first is small, regular and astonishing: a six-pointed star of granite rubble and coral, ramparts a little over four metres thick, a single arched gate faced with coral and lettered with a coat of arms, a set of initials and a year, a chain-operated drawbridge over a ditch about six metres wide and three deep, a glacis of about seven and a half metres outside that, a round well dead in the centre of a courtyard a few strides across, two cells, and twelve positions cut for guns so that every approach is covered from somewhere. It stands a few hundred metres from a much larger and older fort, in the middle of a working provincial town, with a main road along one side of it. It is a protected archaeological monument and a small regional museum in the custody of the state archaeology department. The second is plainer and much more ruined: a square of stone wall about forty-six metres on a side, ramparts five metres high with a walkway along the top, two of its four corners thickened into bastions and the other two left plain, set on a low hill above a river in the interior. Nothing stands inside it now but one building foundation and a large well. Government offices and staff quarters were put up on and around the site in the last century and are still there, and a rural hospital sits just outside the ramparts.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Three things carry it with the sound off, and all three are geometry. From directly overhead at the top of the day, a six-pointed star lying in the middle of an ordinary town, so regular that it reads as a printed diagram rather than a thing made of stone, with a black ditch drawn round the whole outline and roofs, traffic and trees running right up to its edge. From the ditch floor, hard flat light on masonry where every line in the frame is either horizontal or a straight rake — two walls meeting at a point, courses, parapet, ditch floor, and the small dark rectangles cut through the wall for guns. And the cut, fifty kilometres inland, to the other one: a square with two of its corners thickened, standing on a hill with nothing left inside it, filmed on a long lens so the wall and the hill behind it flatten into two bands. The film is deliberately without weather, without low sun and without movement inside the frame; what moves is outside the shape, and it is a town going past.
place.what_moves_or_changes: Almost nothing, and that is the point. The only change inside the frame is the sun, and what it does is move shadow around inside a ditch: at noon the ditch is a black outline and the six angles are invisible, and an hour and a half later the same angles have grown short shadows and the diagram becomes an object. Everything else that moves is on the other side of the ditch — buses, motorcycles, people crossing a pavement, a shop shutter — and none of it looks at the fort. In heavy monsoon rain the fort's own internal drains still put water into the ditch, so there is a chance of standing water and a reflected outline, but this is not something the shoot can count on: the ditch is dry or grassed for most of the year.
place.when_it_looks_best: High, hard, flat daylight, and the drier months. The vertical aerial wants the sun as close to overhead as it can be got, so the shape reads as a shape and not as a set of lit and unlit faces. The ground work wants the same flat light, or plain overcast, which gives clean edges and no drama. This film explicitly does not use golden hour and does not end on a sunset; the one time-of-day change it uses is noon to mid-afternoon, and it uses it only to let shadow appear in the angles. The inland fort is best in the dry months when the grass inside is short enough for the foundation and the well to read from above.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A film about a designed shape, made almost entirely of straight lines and symmetry. It begins with the shape as a diagram seen from straight above, works inwards through the gate and the ditch to the small symmetrical yard and the well at its centre, cuts fifty kilometres inland to a second, cruder version of the same idea with nothing left inside it, and comes back to the first one for a single wide static frame of a stone star with a town walking past it. It resolves on its own terms: diagram, object, ruin, diagram. Someone who hears none of the narration gets a complete piece about geometry, masonry and scale, in hard light, with no crowd, no weather and no golden hour to lean on.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration rather than an argument, and it is the only kind of demonstration this concept can honestly have. The sources describe a state of mind whose name means striking against its object, and they put fear in the same family — the same pushing-away, once the mind has judged the thing too strong and would rather be at a distance from it. Here that movement has been converted into masonry: a shape whose every angle exists so that nothing can approach unseen, costed, contracted and finished in two years, and still standing two hundred and sixty years after the fear, the force it was aimed at and the company that paid for it all ended. The voice never tells the viewer what anyone felt. It says the opposite, and says it out loud: the stone records that something was feared here, and records nothing whatever about anybody's mind — not the garrison's and not the people who took the other fort. What the film can show is the shape, and the shape is legible from the air.

sequence.on_screen: Midday, no cloud. The drone straight down, camera pointing at the ground. In the middle of a working town — roofs, a main road, a bus, a line of trees — one perfectly regular six-pointed star of grey stone, with a ditch running the whole way round its outline. The sun is nearly overhead, so almost nothing in the frame casts a shadow except the ditch, which is black.
sequence.voice: This is a shape before it is a building. It was drawn on paper first: six points, twelve positions cut for guns, every angle set so that nothing can come near any face of it without being in front of somebody. The old books this film is about have a word for the state of mind that meets something it does not like and pushes at it. The word means striking against.

sequence.on_screen: Ground level, flat hard light, dead-on and square: the single gate. A coral-faced stone arch carrying a coat of arms, two initials and a year. The drawbridge deck, the chain slots, the beams projecting above them. Nothing moves in the frame.
sequence.voice: The dates are on record. In 1761 the much larger fort a few hundred metres from here was attacked by forces of the Kandyan kingdom under King Kirti Sri Rajasinha, together with people of the lowlands. The town was shelled from beyond the wall. The Dutch garrison spiked its own guns, destroyed its powder and its stores, and was taken off by two ships waiting at sea. Within two years the Dutch were back, and then they built this. The governor whose name is cut into that arch died in office in the year it was finished.

sequence.on_screen: The outer faces from the ditch floor, long lens, flat light. Two walls meeting at a point, each running away at a rake, and every other line in the frame horizontal: courses, parapet, ditch floor. Then a slow pan along one face to the small dark rectangles cut through it for guns. The ditch is dry and grassed.
sequence.voice: One of these two books is careful about a word most languages keep separate. It puts fear inside the same family as anger: the same pushing-away, once the mind has decided that the thing it dislikes is stronger than it is and had better be kept at a distance. Not a different feeling. The same movement, turned round.

sequence.on_screen: Inside. The courtyard is only a few strides across. A round well head in the middle, shot from directly above so the circle sits inside the six-sided yard. Then the two cells: low doorways, one opening each, flat light. Then a symmetrical wide of the inner faces, left and right identical to within a few centimetres.
sequence.voice: Both books insist on one thing and neither makes an exception to it. This state never arrives without a painful feeling already attached. You can want something and be cheerful the whole time you want it. You cannot do this and feel pleasant. Whatever else it may cost anybody else, it is first of all unpleasant to be inside.

sequence.on_screen: Static wide from across the road: the ditch in the foreground, the near point of the star, traffic crossing the frame and nobody looking. Then long-lens details — grass in the ditch, a drain mouth built through the wall to carry monsoon water out, a plastic bottle in the bottom of it.
sequence.voice: The shorter of the two books lists the ordinary occasions for this state, and the list is domestic. What you asked for was not given. Your word was not accepted. Somebody seems to have done wrong. The older book adds ageing, illness, being parted from what you like, and simply not getting what you want. Not one entry on either list needs a war, and not one of them needs anybody to be a monster.

sequence.on_screen: Straight down again, higher, so the six points read as a diagram with a whole town around them. Held long. Then the identical frame an hour and a half later: the sun has moved, short shadows have grown into the six angles, and the diagram has become an object with thickness.
sequence.voice: There is a list of fourteen of these states, and four of them are said to be present in every unwholesome moment, whatever it looks like from outside. One of the four is a mind that will not settle. That has to be said carefully here. This stone cannot tell us what was in anybody's mind — not the garrison's, not the people who took the other fort. It can only tell us that somebody costed a shape whose entire purpose is that nothing arrives unseen, and got it signed off.

sequence.on_screen: Cut. Fifty kilometres inland: a square of stone wall on a low hill above a river, two of its four corners thickened into bastions and the other two left plain. From directly above, a square with two lumps on opposite ends of one diagonal. Inside it: grass, one building foundation, one large well, nothing else standing. Then a long lens from outside, holding the wall flat against the hill behind it.
sequence.voice: The same year, the same campaign: a smaller fort in the interior was taken and partly pulled down. It had been built eighty years earlier to hold a road. It was repaired and garrisoned again, passed to the British, taken one more time and left. When the kingdom it had been built to watch was annexed and stopped existing, the fort stopped having a point, and it was simply abandoned. The shape is still the shape.

sequence.on_screen: Back at the star, late in a flat overcast afternoon — no low sun, no colour in the sky. One static wide holding the whole shape, the dry ditch, the road and people going past on the pavement without turning their heads. Held for a long time. Then one last vertical, straight down, and the film cuts on it.
sequence.voice: Two hundred and sixty years. The fear this was built out of, the force it was built against, the company that paid for it and the empire that inherited it have all ended, and the angles are still pointing outwards. These books describe single moments of mind, and no camera has ever photographed one. All this stone can tell you is that something here was feared, once, enough to be paid for. What it looks like from directly above is what that feeling looks like if you give it a budget and two years.

concept_merge.why_together: Read fresh, the two digests do different jobs and this location needs both. C007 supplies the definition and the name. Pradeepika defines the state by what it meets and what it wants: a disliked object arrives and the mind strikes against it and wants it destroyed [C007-P:L32–L34]; both sources insist that the two hate-rooted minds always carry a painful mental feeling and are never pleasant, and that they differ from each other only in whether they arise by themselves or after urging [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-M:L3–L9]; and the name itself is physical — paṭigha is striking against the object [C007-P:L34; C007-M:L3]. That is what makes a fort legible rather than decorative: a star fort is a shape built for an object that is not there yet, by people with nothing to strike. C022 supplies the one thing C007 does not say plainly, and it is the thing this building is. Both sources gather fear, discontent, disgust and displeasure inside the same factor as anger, and Pradeepika explains fear as the same recoil once the disliked thing is judged too strong to be gone at [C022-P:L121; C022-M:L35]. Without that line the film would have to call a fortification angry, which is false; with it, the fort is exactly what the source says fear is — the pushing-away, turned round. C022 also gives the four factors said to be present in every unwholesome mind, restlessness among them [C022-P:L31], which is the nearest the sources come to describing pure anticipation, and it gives the guard rail the film needs most: the digest states outright that 'fear is healthy survival instinct' does not map onto this, because the source's word for fear is recoil-aversion while dread of wrongdoing is a different word, praised through the fault of its absence [C022-P:L121; C022-P:L63].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That this state does not have to be caught happening. C007 alone pushes a film towards an incident — a flare, a confrontation, somebody visibly angry — and that is precisely what this group is forbidden to film, because no camera can show which factor is present in a mind. C022 alone is an inventory of fourteen items. Put on these two buildings, the pair produces something neither could: the state as a completed object, with a start date, a finish date, a cost and a surveyor. A six-pointed star is anticipation given a plan, and it is the only thing in this group that can be looked at for two hundred and sixty years without anybody having to be presented as feeling anything. The pairing also fixes the limit that the earlier version of this record broke. The old film ran on an injury nobody could attribute, which invited an audience to read anger onto living, nameable people. Here nobody living is implicated at all, and the film says out loud what the evidence is: masonry records that something was feared, and records nothing about a mind.

concept_links.why: Pradeepika defines the state by its object and its aim — a disliked object is met and the mind wants to destroy it [C007-P:L32–L34] — and both sources make the displeasure constitutive: these two minds always come with a painful mental feeling and never a pleasant one [C007-P:L25–L28; C007-M:L3–L9], so the aversion is suffering before it is anything else, which is the group's own depth line and the only claim the film's fourth beat makes. What makes this location carry the concept rather than resemble it is the name. Margaya explains paṭigha as striking against the object and widens the word to cover anger, grudge, fear, dislike and discontent [C007-M:L3], and Pradeepika uses the same term [C007-P:L34]. A star fort is a shape addressed to an object that has not arrived; there is nothing to strike, only an approach to be anticipated, and the anticipation is the whole design. The occasions are the sources' own: Margaya's list of everyday triggers — what one asks for is not given, one's word is not accepted, others seem to have done wrong [C007-M:L17] — and Pradeepika's afflictions, ageing, illness, separation from what is liked, not getting what one wants [C007-P:L49], which the fifth beat uses to take the film off the battlefield and onto ordinary days. Four limits are load-bearing and are written into the beats and the risks rather than left general. First, Margaya says the hatred felt towards an enemy who comes to harm you is the fierce form of the very same state [C007-M:L11], so the sources grant no exception for being in the right, and a film standing on a site of a real rising must not appear to grant one to either side. Second, the sources say plainly that this state leads on to killing and harming others [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L53], so the film's emphasis on the holder's own displeasure may never be turned into a shrug about what a siege costs. Third, Margaya classes grief at a death as belonging here [C007-M:L19] and Pradeepika counts the death of relatives among the occasions [C007-P:L49]; in ordinary language that sounds cruel, so nothing in this film may imply that anyone who mourned a casualty of 1761 was thereby hateful. Fourth, the sources' only division between the two minds is whether the state arises spontaneously or after urging [C007-P:L38; C007-P:L63; C007-M:L9], and that division is deliberately not applied to a building put up on an order: an instruction to a contractor is not an instance of a mind, and the film says so. Pradeepika's example of a wish turning into the wish to remove a living obstacle [C007-P:L59] is also not imported; there is no living obstacle in this film, and carrying the example across would attribute intentions to historical people that the record does not give.

The digest licenses four things here and nothing else, and being precise about which is the whole value of the link. One: in the list of fourteen, hate is given a far wider range than the English word anger — both sources put fear, discontent, disgust and displeasure inside it, Margaya adds that sorrow arises together with it, and Pradeepika explains fear as aversion once the mind judges the disliked object too strong and wants distance from it [C022-P:L121; C022-M:L35]. That single line is why a defence work can carry this concept honestly instead of being called angry, and it is the third beat. Two: out of the fourteen that both sources list in the same order [C022-P:L31; C022-M:L3], Pradeepika is the one that names four as present in every unwholesome mind, restlessness among them [C022-P:L31] — Margaya leaves that division to a later section, so the claim is Pradeepika's alone and is cited as such. It is as close as these sources come to a description of pure anticipation, and the sixth beat uses it with the limit attached in the same breath. Three: Margaya's account of delusion as what hides the real nature of the object [C022-M:L7] is the reason this film refuses to psychologise anybody at all; what is hidden here is every mind involved, and only the masonry survives. Four, and it is a prohibition rather than a licence: the digest states that 'fear is healthy survival instinct' does not map cleanly onto the source, because the word counted among the forms of aversion is recoil, while dread of wrongdoing is a different word altogether and is praised through the fault of its absence [C022-P:L121; C022-P:L63]. On a fortification that distinction is the difference between a true film and a sneer, and it is why the voice never says that building a wall was a mistake or that prudence is a defilement. Four of the fourteen are explicitly not used, because the digest gives them no purchase here: envy, which takes other people as its object, and stinginess, which takes one's own things [C022-P:L133], have nothing to attach to in an empty fort; remorse, with its teaching that recalling a wrong is not the fault while brooding on it is [C022-P:L143], belonged to the film this record replaces and has been dropped with it; and Pradeepika's moth-and-flame image for fearlessness of wrongdoing [C022-P:L67] is a simile about a moment of mind and would become an accusation if laid over anybody's history. Nothing in this film is stated as a reading of any person's mind, past or present, because the scheme describes single moments of consciousness and a camera cannot see which factor is present in one.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That the sources' word for this state is a physical one — striking against — and that the same movement, once the mind judges the thing too strong to be gone at, is what they call fear. And then the thing the location does that no analogy could: here that movement was drawn on paper, costed, contracted and finished in two years, and it is still standing. Every angle of a six-pointed star exists so that nothing can approach unseen, which makes it pure anticipation in stone. The viewer also gets the limit, which is half the point: the building proves that something was feared and proves nothing at all about what was in anybody's mind. Two hundred and sixty years later the fear has gone, the enemy has gone, the company and the empire have gone, and the shape is exactly where it was.
what_must_be_real: The buildings, their dates and their dimensions. Nothing is re-enacted: no costume, no drill, no torchlit reconstruction, no weapon of any kind handled, carried, loaded or aimed, no cannon fired or simulated, no military display, no drums, no martial music, and no sound design that suggests gunfire, marching or alarm. The 1761 rising is recorded and not adjudicated. The film narrates no side's courage, cruelty, legitimacy or grievance; the rebels are neither heroes nor insurgents and the Dutch are neither villains nor officials doing their duty. The voice gives the sequence of events and the dates and stops there — it deliberately does not narrate a cause, because a cause narrative is exactly where adjudication enters, and what the record gives as the cause is kept in the research block rather than put in anyone's mouth. Casualties are mentioned once or not at all: no figure was found in this research, the recorded facts are a garrison evacuated by sea, its own guns spiked, stores destroyed and buildings burnt, and none of that is the subject of any beat. Neither building is used as a figure for any later conflict in the island's history, and there is no allusion of any kind to the civil war. The floor applies in full. Both sites are protected monuments in state custody and one has working government offices and staff quarters inside its ramparts and a rural hospital immediately outside them: no official, no uniform, no gate, no security post, no office interior, no signage of an occupying institution and no part of the hospital or its grounds appears in a single frame, and no patient, staff member or visitor is filmed. People in the town are filmed as movement on the far side of a ditch, wide and incidental, never as characters and never identifiably, and nobody is filmed who could not meaningfully refuse. No child appears as a character. Museum displays inside the smaller fort may be filmed only as objects and only with the archaeology department's written permission; no visitor or attendant is in frame. If the vertical aerial cannot be permitted, the film is made from the ground and the report says so rather than the film pretending to a view it did not get.
position_hint: Middle-to-late candidate. This is the film for after the heat, and it is the only one in the group with no live human friction in it at all: the state is not caught happening, it is looked at as a finished object with a start date and a completion date. It works best once the group has already shown the same movement arriving and departing in people's working days, so that a shape which has held the posture for two hundred and sixty years lands as a scale change rather than as the first statement. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: The gravest risk is the one that removed the previous version of this record: a war site invites an audience to supply a grievance and a villain. The film records the 1761 sequence and adjudicates nothing, and the voice narrates no side's cause, courage or right.

The righteous-anger reading, which the sources refuse: Margaya names the hatred felt towards an enemy who comes to harm you as the fierce form of the same state [C007-M:L11]. Neither the garrison nor the attackers may be offered that exception, in narration or in edit.

Letting 'aversion hurts the one who holds it' make light of what a siege costs the people in it; the same sources say plainly that this state leads on to killing and harming others [C007-P:L47; C007-P:L53].

Implying that anyone who mourned a death in 1761 was thereby in this state. Margaya technically classes grief at a death here [C007-M:L19] and Pradeepika counts the death of relatives among the occasions [C007-P:L49], and the digest says explicitly that in ordinary language this sounds cruel and false.

Treating a fortification as evidence that its builders were defiled. The digest warns that 'fear is healthy survival instinct' does not map onto the source, because the word counted among the forms of aversion is recoil while dread of wrongdoing is a different word praised through the fault of its absence [C022-P:L121; C022-P:L63]. The film must not read as contempt for prudence.

Reading any mind at all off the stone, living or historical. The scheme describes single moments of consciousness and a camera cannot see which factor is present in one; beat six and beat eight exist to say so out loud.

Narrating Pradeepika's bodily effects of aversion [C007-P:L47], or its claim about such minds at the time of death [C007-P:L51], as observable or medical fact; the digest marks both as doctrinal statements needing expert framing.
Using either building as a metaphor for any later conflict in the island. There is no allusion to the civil war, and the temptation to make one is the reason this is written down.
Any drift towards military aesthetics: re-enactment, weapons, uniforms, drums, low-frequency drone scores, or a cut that makes a gun position look exciting.

The monument-film default, which this group has to avoid: an aerial reveal at golden hour with a slow push. This film is flat noon light, straight lines, static frames and a vertical, and it ends on overcast.
Filming any part of the working institutions on and around the inland site — offices, quarters, the hospital outside the ramparts — or anyone attached to them.

Stating the drier contested details as fact: which bank of the river the smaller fort stands on, whether the Dutch return was 1762 or 1763, when the inland fort was first built, and whether crocodiles were ever kept in the ditch. All four are unresolved and belong in the research block.
drop_if: Neither the vertical aerial nor a usable elevated ground alternative can be obtained, and the six-pointed shape therefore never reads on screen; the whole film is that legibility.
The archaeology department will permit filming only on terms that require an interpretive line about the rising, or only alongside a re-enactment, a costumed guide or a weapons display.
The inland fort cannot be filmed without the working government buildings, their staff or the hospital in frame.
The only way to obtain access is through an institution whose presence in the film would make it look like an official account of a contested episode.

connections.note: Two built lines facing an approach: one a fence and a watch platform where the thing on the other side is alive and still comes, one a geometry where nothing has come for two hundred and sixty years. Opposite treatments as well — night, handheld waiting against flat noon, symmetry and stillness.

Two structures that outlived their purpose: a rail line and pier built towards a crossing that stopped, and a defence built against a force that ceased to exist. Both films end on something still pointing where nothing is.

The slate's other colonial fort film, in a different group and deliberately the opposite piece of cinema: that one is an inventory of what a wall is made of, filmed into dusk with macro work on an opened cross-section; this one refuses substance and films only the designed shape, in hard flat daylight, from directly above.

selection.reason: A location where the concept's own word, striking against, is demonstrated by a shape addressed to an object that never arrived — and a dated, documented sequence in which a fort fell and the answer was a geometry with a budget and a completion date.

review.note: Rewritten completely onto a new location and a new argument; the previous film is gone for two reasons, both of which were disqualifying. The first is the group's monoculture: eleven of GRP-03's fourteen films were working places with no historical story in them, and a group cannot be a monoculture, so this record had to become a dated and documented film. The second is more serious than that and is the reason the old film could not simply be improved. Its engine was a grievance — a fishing net torn by a boat nobody could name, in a former conflict zone, repaired over three days — and this group's concepts are the hate-rooted minds. A film whose motor is an unattributable injury to real, nameable, living fishers invites the audience to read anger onto them, which the floor forbids outright: no identifiable person may be presented as angry, because no camera can show which mental factor is present in a mind. It went, and nothing of it is recoverable. In its place: two colonial defence works in the far south, a six-pointed star fort with a moat, a drawbridge and twelve gun positions, and a small square fort with two bastions fifty kilometres inland, bound together by a verified sequence — in 1761 the main coastal fort was taken in the rising and the Dutch were forced out, the interior forts were overrun, the Dutch returned and from 1763 to 1765 built a second, smaller fort expressly to protect the main one from attack off the river. So the film has a fort that fell and, as the answer, a geometry with a start date, a finish date and a surveyor: aversion converted into masonry and left standing for two hundred and sixty years, outliving the fear, the enemy and the empire. The philosophical work is done on the sources rather than by analogy: C007 for the state named after striking against an object, always accompanied by displeasure, applied to a shape built for an object that had not arrived; C022 for the one line that makes a defence work legible instead of slanderous, that fear is the same aversion once the thing is judged too strong to be gone at, plus the four factors present in every unwholesome moment. The limit is written into the film twice rather than left to a caution: the stone records that something was feared and records nothing about anybody's mind, the garrison's or the rebels'. The 1761 rising is a nationalist touchstone and the film is neutral by construction — the voice gives the sequence and the dates, narrates no side's cause, courage, cruelty or legitimacy, and deliberately does not state a cause at all, because the causal narrative is where adjudication enters; the recorded cause is held in the research block instead. No re-enactment, no weapons, no military display, no drums or martial music, and no allusion to any later conflict in the island. New title, with the previous titles kept in aliases. Both concept links were re-tested line by line against their digests and rewritten, including four C022 factors explicitly withdrawn as unlicensed here. New place block, new two_layers, eight new beats, and a fully researched location with a historical_thread and nine verified Commons images. Because the body is rewritten, the verdict resets to pending.

suggested_location.name: The Star Fort at Matara (originally Redoute Van Eck) and the Dutch fort at Katuwana

also_known_as.name: Redoute Van Eck
also_known_as.meaning: the redoubt of Van Eck, after Lubbert Jan baron van Eck, Dutch Governor of Ceylon; the name and the year are cut into the gate arch
also_known_as.used_by: the Dutch East India Company, and the fort's own inscription

also_known_as.name: Star Fort
also_known_as.meaning: the six-pointed plan; the name in ordinary English and signage use today
also_known_as.used_by: the Department of Archaeology and local usage

also_known_as.name: Fort Catoene, Cattoene, Katoene, Catuna
also_known_as.meaning: Dutch and German renderings of Katuwana in eighteenth-century VOC maps, plans and published views
also_known_as.used_by: VOC cartography and eighteenth-century travel publication

suggested_location.region: Matara District, Southern Province — the Star Fort stands in Matara town, a few hundred metres from the main Matara fort — together with the Dutch fort at Katuwana, about fifty kilometres north-east and inland, in the Hambantota District of the same province

secondary_coordinates.note: The Dutch fort at Katuwana, on a low hill above the east bank of the Urubokka Oya, Katuwana town, Hambantota District. Published as 6.26750 N, 80.69500 E and as 6.2674748 N, 80.6952774 E; the two agree to within about thirty metres.

suggested_location.why_here: Because the history here is the argument rather than a resemblance to it, and because the argument is only legible from the air. A fort fell in 1761 and the recorded answer to that was a shape: a six-pointed star with a moat and a drawbridge, begun in 1763 and finished in 1765, built expressly to protect the main fort from attack coming off the river. That is aversion with a start date, a completion date, a budget and a surveyor, and it is still standing two hundred and sixty years later, long after the fear, the force it was aimed at, the company that paid for it and the empire that inherited it have all ended. No working place can carry that, because no working place has a dated document in which somebody decided what fear should be shaped like. The site also gives the film its one indispensable frame: a star fort's whole logic — that no approach is unobserved — exists only in plan, so the vertical aerial is not a flourish but the statement of the concept, and it is surrounded by a town that walks past it without looking. The second location does the work the first cannot. The inland fort is cruder, older and ruined, was taken in the same campaign and partly pulled down, was garrisoned again, and was finally abandoned when the kingdom it had been built to watch was annexed and ceased to exist. One shape outlived its fear in good repair and one outlived it as a wall with nothing inside; between them they say what a single site could not, which is that the shape does not depend on the fear to keep standing. And the pair is neutral by construction: both are empty of the living, so nobody can be presented as angry, which is the constraint that governs this whole group.
what_to_film: The vertical aerial at the top of the day: the six-pointed star from directly overhead, with the ditch drawn black round the outline and a town running up to its edge. This is the film's statement of its concept and everything else is built around getting it.

The same vertical frame repeated ninety minutes later, so that shadow has entered the six angles and the diagram becomes an object with thickness. The cut between the two is the film's only use of changing light.
The gate dead-on and square in flat light: the coral-faced arch, the coat of arms, the initials and the year, the drawbridge deck, the chain slots and the beams above them. No low-angle heroics.
The outer faces from the ditch floor on a long lens, composed so that every line is either horizontal or a straight rake, and the gun openings read as small dark rectangles in a flat wall.

The ditch itself along its whole circuit: dry, grassed, with the built drain mouths that carry the fort's own monsoon water into it. If heavy rain has left standing water, one frame of the outline reflected — as a contingency, not a plan.
The interior: the well head from directly above so the circle sits inside the six-sided yard, the two cells, and one symmetrical wide of the inner faces.

Museum objects inside the fort, as objects only and only if written permission allows: the Dutch survey drawings, scaled models and excavated material, filmed flat-on with no attendant and no visitor in frame.
The town's indifference in one static wide from across the road, with traffic and pedestrians crossing on the far side of the ditch, incidental and unidentifiable, nobody in the frame as a character.
The inland fort from directly above: a square about forty-six metres on a side with two diagonally opposite corners thickened, grass inside, one building foundation and one large well.

The inland fort's rampart on a long lens from outside, flattened against the hill behind it, and the reconstructed arched entrance, with the modern government buildings and the hospital kept wholly out of frame.

If the vertical aerial is refused, the ground fallback and nothing dressed up as more than it is: the rampart walkway itself, and the highest lawful neighbouring vantage obtainable by private agreement, accepting that the six points will then read as a run of angles rather than as one shape.

historical_thread.story:
In December 1760 a rising against the Dutch East India Company broke out in the Company's lowland territories in Ceylon and ran through the following year. It began in districts bordering the Kandyan Kingdom and spread along the coast. The Dutch interior posts at Hanwella and Katuwana were overrun, and in 1761 the main Dutch fort at Matara was attacked by forces of the Kandyan Kingdom under King Kirti Sri Rajasinha together with lowland people who had joined them. The record of the attack is that the town was bombarded with cannonballs that went over the wall; that the Dutch garrison spiked its own cannon and destroyed its ammunition and provisions before being evacuated by two ships waiting offshore; and that the fort was afterwards burnt. The Dutch were out of Matara. Lubbert Jan baron van Eck, born at Velp on 26 March 1719, had been appointed Governor of Ceylon on 29 May 1761 and took up the office on 18 February 1762, in the middle of a war with Kandy that ran to 1766. He retook Matara and Hanwella; Dutch accounts put the recapture of the Matara fort on 2 February 1762, and eight cannon were found on its walls, one of them English. An expedition into the interior in 1763 failed against Kandyan guerrilla tactics, and peace talks the same year came to nothing.

What the Dutch did next at Matara is the reason this film exists. Having got the main fort back, they built a second and much smaller one a few hundred metres away, across the river, for the single declared purpose of protecting the main fort against attack coming from the river. Construction ran from 1763 to 1765. It was a six-pointed star with a moat and a chain-operated drawbridge, and it was named Redoute Van Eck after the governor. The gate arch, faced with coral, carries the VOC insignia of the Dutch East India Company in its pediment, a coat of arms flanked by lions, the governor's initials and the year 1763. The fort has space for twelve large cannon covering every approach, with embrasures cut through the parapet; the rampart walls are of granite rubble and coral and about 4.3 metres thick; the glacis outside the ditch is about 7.5 metres wide and the ditch itself about 6 metres wide and 3.1 metres deep; there is a well 2.75 metres in diameter in the centre of the courtyard to supply the garrison, two prison cells, and stores for food and ammunition sufficient to hold out until the main fort could reinforce it. Its drainage was internal and put monsoon water into the moat. The roof was originally of cadjan leaf and was later tiled. Van Eck did not see it finished as a garrisoned post for long: he died in office in Colombo on 1 April 1765, the year the fort bearing his name was completed, while conducting a second invasion of the Kandyan kingdom.

After 1765 the fort served as barracks and an officer's residence. The Dutch surrendered their territories to the British in 1796 and the building became official housing, then a public library run by the Matara Urban Council, recorded as in use from about 1965. It had been declared an archaeological protected monument by government gazette notification on 26 March 1959, and it passed into the custody of the Department of Archaeology in 1980. Modern accretions were removed in a campaign of works in the later 1980s, it was converted to a museum of art history in 1991, and a conservation and landscaping project funded by the Netherlands embassy in Colombo ran from March 2000 to March 2007, whose chief achievement was the restoration of the drawbridge — described as the only surviving Dutch drawbridge on public display in Sri Lanka. It now holds a small regional museum of the archaeology of the southern region, with material from prehistoric, Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa, Kandyan and colonial periods. The ditch survives but is dry, and has been partly filled by the earth of the banks outside it.

The interior fort at Katuwana sits about fifty kilometres north-east of Matara, in the Hambantota District, on a low hill on the east bank of the Urubokka Oya, in what was the Dolosdahas Korale. It was built to hold the route between Kandy and Matara and to protect Dutch commerce along it — an inland fort aimed at the Kandyan kingdom rather than a coastal one aimed at European rivals. The earliest record of a field fortification there is 1661, and a stone fort was built in 1679–1680. It is a square of about 46 by 46 metres with two diagonally opposite bastions, ramparts about 5 metres high outside and 2.4 to 3.7 metres inside, with a walkway about 4 metres wide on top, a single gateway, and boulder-built walls; the two bastions carried twelve cannon between them. A 1695 Dutch plan lists the guardroom, two sergeants' rooms, a small house for the constable, an arsenal, a powder house, a provisions store and a well; a 1736 published ground plan of the same fort names much the same rooms and adds a surgeon's lodging. In 1761, in the same Matara offensive, Kandyan forces captured the fort and partly destroyed it. It was under British control from 1796, was captured once more by a Kandyan army in 1805 and then abandoned by them, and after the British annexation of the Kandyan kingdom in 1815 it lost its strategic value altogether and was given up. It was declared a protected monument in 1980. In January and February 2000 it became the first site in Sri Lanka to be scientifically excavated for its colonial-period archaeology, in a joint project of the Postgraduate Institute of Archaeology at the University of Kelaniya and the Amsterdam Archaeological Centre at the University of Amsterdam, led by S. Lakdusinghe, Anura Manatunga and H. A. Heidinga; about fifteen per cent of the site was opened. Indigenous earthenware made up 83.3 per cent of the artefact fragments, with European red-glazed earthenware, glass bottles, clay tobacco pipes and Chinese porcelain among the rest, including one complete porcelain bowl. In 2007 the arched entrance was excavated and rebuilt by the Department of Archaeology using traditional craftsmanship, with Netherlands assistance, and there were plans to move the government buildings off the site. Nothing of the interior ranges now stands: one building foundation in the south-east corner and a large well in the north-west are what is left. A rural hospital was built just outside the ramparts in the early twentieth century, and a local administrative centre, assistant government agents' offices, residences and other government buildings were put up inside the fort.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C007 names the state after a physical action. Paṭigha is striking against the object, and Pradeepika defines the state by the meeting: a disliked object arrives and the mind goes at it, wanting it gone. Everything in that definition needs an object. This history is the one case where the object is absent and the movement is nevertheless fully visible, because it was built.

Begin with the sequence, because the sequence is what no analogy can supply. A fort was lost in 1761. Within two years the same power was back on the same ground, and the first thing it did with the ground was to draw a shape. Not a wall, not a bigger fort — a six-pointed star, whose entire geometric purpose is that every face of it is enfiladed from somewhere else, so that no approach is unobserved. It was surveyed, costed, contracted and finished between 1763 and 1765, and the stated reason was an attack that might come off the river. That is anticipation with a completion date. It is the nearest thing in the island's documentary record to a fear that can be measured with a tape: 4.3 metres of rampart, a ditch 6 metres wide and 3.1 deep, a glacis of 7.5 metres, twelve positions for guns. The film does not have to argue that fear takes shapes. Somebody wrote the shape down and then built it, and the drawing survives in an archive alongside the thing itself.

C022 is what makes this legible rather than slanderous. Left to C007 alone the film would have to call a fortification angry, which is false and would also be an accusation against historical people. But the fourteen-factor list puts fear inside the same factor as anger and explains why: it is the same recoil, once the mind has judged the disliked thing too strong to be gone at and wants distance from it instead. A star fort is precisely distance, organised. Its angles are not for attacking anybody; they are for making sure nothing gets close. So the building is not an image of rage, it is an image of the source's own account of fear — aversion that has decided to keep the object at arm's length — and that account is the only reason the concept and this masonry are the same subject. The same list supplies the other half: four factors are said to be in every unwholesome moment, and one of them is a mind that will not settle. Pure anticipation has no event in it. It is a posture held towards something that has not happened, and this one has been held for two hundred and sixty years.

Then the outliving, which is where the two sites do what one could not. The Company that ordered the smaller fort is gone. The kingdom it was aimed at is gone. The empire that inherited it is gone. The fort is a museum, the ditch is dry and grassed, the drawbridge has been restored with money from the country whose company built it, and the angles still point outwards. Fifty kilometres inland the same idea is visible without any of the upkeep: a square of boulders with two of its corners thickened, standing on a hill above a river, which was taken and partly pulled down in the same campaign, repaired, garrisoned, taken again, and finally abandoned outright when the kingdom it had been built to watch was annexed in 1815 and simply stopped existing. There is nothing inside it now but a well and a foundation. The pair makes the point precise: the fear ended, the object of the fear ended, and the shape did not need either of them in order to remain. Both sources say the state itself is always accompanied by displeasure and never pleasant — it is suffering before it is anything else, felt first by whoever holds it. What outlasts it is not the feeling. It is the geometry the feeling paid for.

And the limit, which is why this location is right and not merely striking. Stone is evidence of exactly one thing: that somebody judged an approach dangerous enough to spend two years on. It is not evidence about a mind. The sources describe single moments of consciousness, a camera cannot see which factor is present in one, and no document from 1761 or 1763 records what any garrison soldier or any attacker felt. So the film's strongest move is a refusal: it says out loud that the building records a fear and records nothing about the people, on either side, and that the rising itself is a sequence of recorded events which this film will not adjudicate. That refusal is not caution bolted on. It is the same doctrine the film is teaching, applied to the film's own evidence — a scheme about moments of mind cannot be read off a wall, however eloquent the wall.
what_is_certain: A rising against the Dutch East India Company in its lowland Ceylon territories broke out in December 1760 and continued through 1761, beginning in districts bordering the Kandyan Kingdom and spreading along the coast.

The Dutch posts at Hanwella and Katuwana were overrun by the rebels, and in 1761 the main Dutch fort at Matara was attacked by forces of the Kandyan Kingdom under King Kirti Sri Rajasinha, joined by lowland people. The recorded account of the attack is that the town was bombarded with cannonballs that went over the wall, that the Dutch garrison spiked its own cannon and destroyed its ammunition and provisions before being evacuated by two ships waiting at sea, and that the fort was burnt afterwards.
Eight cannon, one of them English, were found on the walls of the Matara fort when the Dutch returned.

Lubbert Jan baron van Eck was born at Velp, Gelderland, on 26 March 1719, was appointed Governor of Ceylon on 29 May 1761, took up office on 18 February 1762, and died in office at Colombo on 1 April 1765 while conducting a second invasion of the Kandyan kingdom.

Having regained the main fort at Matara, the Dutch built a second, much smaller fort nearby for the express purpose of protecting the main fort from attack originating from the river. Construction ran from 1763 to 1765.

That fort is a six-pointed star with a moat and a chain-operated drawbridge, and was originally named Redoute Van Eck after the governor. The coral-faced gate arch carries the VOC insignia of the Dutch East India Company in its pediment, a coat of arms flanked by lions, the governor's initials and the year 1763.

It has space for twelve large cannon covering approaches from all directions, with embrasures cut for them; rampart walls of granite and coral about 14 feet (4.3 m) thick; a glacis about 7.5 m (25 ft) wide; a ditch about 6 m (20 ft) wide and 3.1 m (10 ft) deep; a well 2.75 m (9 ft) in diameter in the centre of the courtyard; two prison cells; and stores for food and ammunition sufficient for a small garrison to hold out until reinforced from the main fort. Its drainage was internal and discharged monsoon water into the moat. Its roof was originally of cadjan leaf and was later tiled.

After completion the fort served as barracks and an officer's residence; it passed to the British with the Dutch surrender of 1796 and was used as official housing, and by about 1965 as the public library of the Matara Urban Council.

It was declared an archaeological protected monument by government gazette notification of 26 March 1959, and came into the custody of the Department of Archaeology in 1980. Modern structures were removed in works of the later 1980s; it was converted to a museum in 1991; and a conservation and landscaping project funded by the Embassy of the Netherlands in Colombo ran from March 2000 to March 2007, whose principal achievement was the restoration of the drawbridge, described as the only surviving Dutch drawbridge on public display in Sri Lanka.

It now houses a small regional museum of the archaeology of the southern region, run by the Department of Archaeology, with material of prehistoric, Anuradhapura, Polonnaruwa, Kandyan and colonial date. The ditch survives but is dry, and has been partly filled by earth from the banks outside it.

The Dutch fort at Katuwana lies about fifty kilometres north-east of Matara, in the Hambantota District, on a low hill on the east bank of the Urubokka Oya, in the historical Dolosdahas Korale. It was built to secure the route between Kandy and Matara and to protect Dutch commerce along it, facing the Kandyan kingdom inland rather than a European rival at sea.

It is a square fort of about 46 by 46 metres (150 by 150 feet) with two diagonally opposite bastions, built of large stone boulders, with ramparts about 5 m (16 ft) high externally and 2.4 to 3.7 m internally, a walkway about 4 m (13 ft) wide on top, and a single gateway. The two bastions carried twelve cannon between them. Its modest scale has led writers to describe it as a redoubt rather than a fort.

A Dutch plan of 1695 lists a guardroom, two sergeants' rooms, a small house for the constable, an arsenal, a powder house, a provisions store and a well; a published ground plan of 1736 names much the same rooms and adds a surgeon's lodging.

In 1761, in the same Matara offensive, Kandyan forces captured the Katuwana fort and partly destroyed it. It was under British control from 1796, was captured once more by a Kandyan army in 1805 and then abandoned by them, and after the British annexation of the Kandyan kingdom in 1815 it lost its strategic value and was abandoned.

Katuwana was declared a protected monument in 1980. In January and February 2000 it was excavated by a joint project of the Postgraduate Institute of Archaeology (University of Kelaniya) and the Amsterdam Archaeological Centre (University of Amsterdam), led by S. Lakdusinghe, Anura Manatunga and H. A. Heidinga — reported as the first site in the country excavated scientifically for its colonial-period archaeology. About fifteen per cent of the site was opened. Indigenous earthenware made up 83.3 per cent of artefact fragments; European red-glazed earthenware, glass bottles, clay tobacco pipes and Chinese porcelain were also found, including one complete Chinese porcelain bowl.

In 2007 the arched entrance of the Katuwana fort was excavated and rebuilt by the Department of Archaeology using traditional craftsmanship, with assistance from the Netherlands, and relocation of the government buildings on the site was planned.

Nothing of Katuwana's internal ranges stands: one building foundation in the south-east corner and a large well in the north-west remain. A rural hospital was built just outside the ramparts in the early twentieth century, and a local administrative centre, assistant government agents' offices and residences and other government buildings were built inside the fort.

Drone operation over an archaeological site in Sri Lanka requires a no-objection letter from the Department of Archaeology as well as Ministry of Defence security clearance and Civil Aviation Authority operating approval, with third-party liability insurance.
what_is_disputed: The year the Dutch regained Matara. Accounts of the Star Fort say the Dutch regained control in 1763 and began the new fort that year; the account of the main fort and the biography of the governor both give the recapture as 2 February 1762, with Matara and Hanwella retaken in 1762. The construction dates 1763 to 1765 are consistent across sources; the recapture year is not, and this film does not resolve it.

Which bank of the river the Star Fort stands on. One standard reference says the east bank; a detailed site account says the western bank, about 400 metres from the main fort; and the title of an 1888 drawing of the fort says the northern bank of the river and north-west of the fort. The distance is given as 350 metres in one account and 400 in another.

The completion date carried by the building itself. The gate arch bears 1763, and 1765 is the date usually given for completion; one account says 1765 is embossed on the main entrance arch. Both years appear on or about the gate in different retellings.

When the drawbridge was restored. A conservation project account puts the restored drawbridge within a programme running to March 2007, with handover in July 2008; another account dates the restoration to 2012 with Dutch government support. A photograph of 2008 already shows a chain-operated drawbridge in place.

When the Katuwana fort was first built. Sources give 1645, 1646, and a field fortification first recorded in 1661 followed by a stone fort of 1679–1680 or 1679–1681. The 1679–1680 stone fort is the best-attested; the earlier dates are not reconciled.

Whether crocodiles were kept in the Star Fort's moat as a deterrent. This appears in visitor and image-description writing and in popular accounts. No archival source for it was found in this research and it is not used in the film.

Who built the Star Fort on the ground. One detailed account credits a headman titled Orukema Muhandiram with the construction under the governor's authority. This was not corroborated elsewhere and is not used in the voice.

The recorded cause of the 1760–61 rising. It is given in the secondary literature as a Dutch attempt to register peasants' landholdings and either dispossess them or tax them, with Kandyan forces joined by rebellious lowlanders. That is the recorded cause; whether it was the whole of it, and how the responsibility for the war should be apportioned, is an interpretive question this film does not enter. The rising is a nationalist touchstone, and the record here is held as record.

Casualties. No casualty figure for the fall of the Matara fort, the overrunning of Katuwana or the Dutch return was found in this research. What is recorded is a garrison evacuated by sea after spiking its guns and destroying its stores, a town bombarded, and a fort burnt. Absence of a figure is not evidence that there were none, and the film does not supply one.

Above all: none of this adjudicates the 1761 rising, and the film does not adjudicate it. What the record establishes is a sequence of events and a set of dated buildings. It says nothing about which side was in the right, and no side's courage, cruelty or legitimacy is narrated. Where the meaning of the rising is contested, that it is contested is the finding.

suggested_location.access: The Star Fort stands in the middle of Matara town, a short walk from the main fort, on a public road, and is open to visitors as a Department of Archaeology museum — reported as Wednesday to Monday, roughly 09:00 to 16:30, with an entrance charge. It is a protected archaeological monument, so any filming beyond a visitor's snapshot, and certainly any drone work, requires written permission from the Department of Archaeology; drone flight additionally requires Ministry of Defence security clearance submitted several days in advance with the department's no-objection letter, Civil Aviation Authority operating approval and third-party insurance. Katuwana is reached by road from the interior of the Hambantota District, conveniently from the Middeniya side; it is also a protected monument and the same permissions apply. Katuwana carries a second and harder access problem: working government offices, staff residences and an administrative centre stand inside the ramparts and a rural hospital immediately outside them, so a shooting plan has to be agreed in advance that keeps all of them, and everyone attached to them, entirely out of frame. No permission of any kind has been sought or confirmed.
suggested_location.best_time: The drier months, and the middle of the day. The vertical aerial wants the sun as near overhead as it can be got, so the star reads as a plan rather than as lit and unlit faces, and the ground work wants the same hard flat light or a plain overcast. The one deliberate change of light is noon to mid-afternoon, for shadow to enter the six angles. There is no golden-hour or sunset element in this film and none should be shot as a safety net. Katuwana is best in the dry months, when the grass inside the ramparts is short enough for the well and the foundation to read from above; the monsoon months are the only time the Star Fort's ditch might hold standing water, and that possibility is a contingency rather than a plan.

suggested_location.research_note: All of this is desk research by web search on 25 September 2026 and none of it has been checked on the ground, against a printed edition or against an archive. The construction dates 1763–1765, the six-pointed plan, the moat, the drawbridge, the twelve gun positions, the rampart thickness, the glacis and ditch dimensions, the central well, the two cells, the internal drainage, the gate inscription, the 1959 gazette protection, the 1980 transfer to the Department of Archaeology, the 1991 museum conversion, the Netherlands-funded conservation of 2000–2007 and the fort's present use as a regional museum are all from the sources listed and cross-read between at least two of them where possible. The Katuwana dimensions, the two diagonally opposite bastions, the 1695 and 1736 plans, the 1761 capture and partial destruction, the 1805 capture, the abandonment after 1815, the 1980 protection, the 2000 excavation and its finds, the 2007 entrance reconstruction and the government buildings and hospital on and around the site come from the same kind of reading. Where sources disagree — the year of the Dutch return, which bank of the river the Star Fort stands on, the date on the gate against the completion date, when the drawbridge was restored, and the first construction date at Katuwana — the disagreement is recorded in what_is_disputed and is not resolved. The crocodile story and the named local builder of the Star Fort were each found in only one kind of source and are not used. No casualty figure for 1761 was found anywhere in this research, which is why the film records the evacuation and the burning and no number. The moat is dry today, partly filled by earth from the banks outside it, so the still-water frame this treatment would like is a monsoon contingency and not a plan; that is written into best_time and what_to_film rather than assumed. Coordinates for the Star Fort are the published 5°56′53″N 80°32′54″E; the elevation figure is a rough estimate for a coastal town site and was not verified, and no elevation was found for Katuwana. Commons holds good modern photographs of the Star Fort and, so far as this search could establish, no modern photograph of the Katuwana fort at all: the three Katuwana images listed are eighteenth-century archival plans and views and their captions say so explicitly, and no photograph of any other place has been substituted. Every one of the nine files was confirmed to exist through the Commons query API before its URL was written. Access, permissions, opening hours, museum filming terms, drone clearance and the present state of both ditches are unverified.

unknowns: No permission of any kind has been sought or confirmed. Both sites are protected archaeological monuments, so filming beyond a visitor's snapshot needs written Department of Archaeology permission, and nothing here establishes that it would be given.

The drone is the film's natural frame and its permission is the single largest unknown. Flying over an archaeological site requires a departmental no-objection letter, Ministry of Defence security clearance submitted several days ahead, Civil Aviation Authority operating approval and third-party insurance, and any one of those can be refused. It is also a vertical flight over the middle of a populated town, which raises its own objections. The honest ground fallback — the rampart walkway plus the highest neighbouring vantage obtainable by private agreement — does not deliver the six-pointed shape as one object, and the film would be weaker in a way the report should state plainly rather than disguise.

Whether the inland fort can be filmed at all without the working government offices, staff residences or the rural hospital appearing in frame, and whether a shooting plan on those terms would be agreed.
Whether the ditch at either site ever holds standing water in a filmable way, and if so in which weeks.
Whether the eighteenth-century Dutch plan of the fort can be used on screen at all — the original is in a European state archive, and reproduction terms for a film were not checked.
Whether the museum inside the fort would permit filming of its objects and survey drawings, and on what conditions.

Whether the discrepancies recorded in what_is_disputed — chiefly the 1762 against 1763 recapture and the bank of the river — can be settled from Dutch archival sources. They have not been, and the film is written so that nothing depends on settling them.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The two locations are Claude's suggestion and await Chathura's verdict; all supporting detail is desk research from web sources and is unverified on the ground, in print or in any archive. The 1761 rising is recorded here as a sequence of documented events and is deliberately not adjudicated. No scene or shot is decided here.
